title: The Winning of a Queen: Chapter 3
paragraphs: _How King Arthur Met Four Knights and What Happened Because of It._

The day was wonderfully sweet and pleasant for a man as strong in body and light of heart as good King Arthur. Bright clouds sailed smoothly across the blue sky in huge billows of vapor. The wind blew across the long grass of the meadows and the fields of growing wheat, so that waves ran over the hills and valleys as if across a whole sea of green. At one moment the whole earth would be darkened by the wide shadows of those clouds, and the next moment everything would burst out again into a wonderful blaze of sunlight. The little birds sang merrily in the hedgerows and the leafy thickets, as though they would burst their tiny throats with singing. The rooster crowed, strong and bold, from the farmyard. All was so cheerful and lovely that the young King, with the visor of his helmet raised to feel the gentle breeze, would sometimes sing aloud for joy as he traveled. So King Arthur journeyed through that gay and tender summer season, when the earth was young and the time was long ago.

Now, remember that when King Arthur came from Carleon to the castle of Tintagalon, he had brought four young knights with him to keep him company. Those knights were these. There was Sir Gawaine, the son of King Lot and Queen Margaise. There was Sir Ewaine, the son of King Uriens and Queen Morgana la Fay (these two were nephews of the King, half related by blood). There was Sir Pellias, and there was Sir Geraint, the son of Erbin. These were the four noble young knights who had come with King Arthur from Camelot to Tintagalon.

As King Arthur rode along happily in the summer weather, he came to a place on the road where he saw a tall and handsome tower standing on a green hill right beside the road. And look! On the balcony of that tower stood three fair young ladies, all dressed in green taffeta. On the high road in front of the castle was a knight in very fine armor. He sat on a noble war-horse, and in his hands he held a lute. He played the lute and sang in a voice of wonderful sweetness. While he sang, the three ladies in green taffeta listened to him with cheerful faces. Whenever the knight stopped singing, the three ladies clapped their hands loudly and asked him to sing to them again, and he gladly did so.
King Arthur saw all this, and it seemed to him a very pleasant sight, so he was greatly delighted by it.

As he came closer, he saw that the knight who sat on his horse, playing the lute and singing to its music, was none other than Sir Geraint, the son of Erbin. That knight wore the figure of a gryphon on his crest, and the design on his shield was two gryphons standing on their hind legs, facing each other on a blue field. King Arthur knew that these were the crest and the shield of Sir Geraint. When the King saw who the singing knight was, he laughed to himself, quickly closed his visor, and made himself ready for whatever fight might come. Then he rode up to where the knight sang and the ladies listened.

When Sir Geraint saw King Arthur approaching, he stopped singing and hung his lute behind him across his shoulder. Then he looked up at the three fair ladies above him and said, “Ladies, you have been kind enough to listen to the song that I sang entirely in your honor. Now, in your honor as well, I will perform a deed of knightly courage, and I very much hope it will bring you great glory. If you will give me the encouragement that your great beauty can so easily offer, I have no doubt that you will see me defeat that knight over there completely. It will be to your great credit and fame.”

“Sir Knight,” said the lady who spoke for the others, “you are truly a lord of noble bearing and very pleasing manners, so we wish you great success in this task. We believe that you will succeed in what you attempt.”

Sir Geraint thanked the three young ladies warmly for their words, and then he closed the visor of his helmet. He lowered his spear, readied his shield, and bowed humbly to the three ladies. Then he rode out to meet King Arthur, who sat a short distance away, quietly and calmly waiting for him.

Sir Geraint did not recognize King Arthur, because the King wore no crest on his helmet and no design on his shield. As he saluted him, he spoke to him like this: “Ha! Good sir, I do not know who you are, since you carry neither crest nor shield design. Even so, I wish to do you the honor of riding a tilt with you on behalf of those three young ladies that you see on that balcony. I declare, and I am ready to defend my words in person as a knight, that those ladies are fairer than your lady, whoever she may be.”

“Sir Knight,” said King Arthur, “I will gladly ride a course with you in honor of my lady. I can tell you that she is a princess, and many people consider her the most beautiful lady in all the world. But I will fight you only on one condition. The one who is thrown from his horse must give himself as a servant to the other for seven days, and during that time he must do everything that is asked of him.”

“I accept your challenge, Sir Unknown Knight,” said Sir Geraint, “and when I have thrown you down, I will hand you over to those fair ladies over there to be their servant for seven days. I tell you that many knights would certainly think that a pleasant and honorable task.”

“And if I should happen to throw you down,” said King Arthur, “I will send you to serve my lady for the same length of time. That will be an even more pleasant and honorable task than the one you have in mind for me.”

So each knight saluted the other, and then each took his place so that the clash would happen right below the balcony where the three fair young ladies looked down. Each knight lowered his spear and readied his shield, and when they were prepared, each sat still for a short moment. Then each shouted to his war-horse, dug his spurs into its flanks, and charged forward with amazing speed. They met in the very middle of the course with a force so fierce that the noise of it was terrifying to hear. Each knight struck the other in the very center of his defenses. And look! The spear of Sir Geraint burst into small pieces, all the way down to the stump. But the spear of King Arthur held firm, and Sir Geraint was thrown so violently backward that he and his horse both crashed into the dust with a noise like a huge roar of thunder.

When Sir Geraint got back on his feet, he was so astonished for a while that he did not know where he stood, because he had never been thrown like that in all his life. Then he quickly came to his senses, drew his sword at once, and called out fiercely for King Arthur to come down from his saddle and fight him on foot.

“No, Sir Knight,” said King Arthur, “I will not fight you that way. And do not forget that you promised to give yourself to me as my servant for seven days. I have clearly beaten you in this encounter, and now you are pledged to be my servant.”

Then Sir Geraint did not know what to say, for he was completely overcome with shame and anger at his defeat. Still, he saw that he must keep his knightly word and do what he had promised. So he put his sword away again, though he was very unhappy about it. “Sir Knight,” he said, “I admit that I have been beaten in this encounter, so I place myself under your commands, as I promised.”

“Then this is my command to you,” said King Arthur. “You must go at once to the Lady Guinevere at Cameliard and tell her that you were thrown down by the knight to whom she gave her necklace as a token. I also want you to obey her in everything she commands you to do, for the next seven days.”
“Sir Knight,” said Sir Geraint, “I will do what you ask of me, as you command.”

Then he mounted his horse and went on his way, and King Arthur went on his way too. The three ladies who stood on the balcony of the castle were very glad that they had seen such a noble contest of arms as the one they had looked down upon.

After King Arthur had traveled two or three leagues or more, he came to a place of moorland, where there were many ditches full of water and where the heron and the marsh-hen hid in the reeds. Here and there stood several windmills, their sails turning slowly in the sunlight before a wind that blew across the level plains of mud. At this place there was a long, straight causeway with two long rows of pollard willows, one on each side. When he had come near the middle of this causeway, King Arthur saw two knights sitting on their horses in the shade of a great windmill that stood beside the road. A large shadow of the sails moved across the road from time to time as the wheel of the mill turned slowly in the wind. All around the mill, and everywhere about, were great numbers of swallows that darted this way and that like bees around a hive in midsummer. King Arthur saw that the two knights, as they sat in the shadow of the mill, were eating a large loaf of rye bread, freshly baked with a crisp crust. They also ate fine white cheese, and the miller, all white with flour dust, served these things to them. But when the two knights saw King Arthur, they stopped eating the bread and cheese at once and quickly closed their helmets. When the miller saw them getting ready, he hurried back into the mill and shut the door. Then he went and looked out of a window above the place where the knights stood.

King Arthur was very amused when he saw that the two knights were Sir Gawaine and Sir Ewaine. He knew that one was Sir Gawaine because the crest of his helmet was a leopard standing on its hind legs, and because the design on his shield was a leopard standing on its hind legs on a red field. He knew that the other was Sir Ewaine, because his crest was a unicorn, and because the design on his shield was a lady holding a bare sword in her hand, on a gold field. So while he was still some way off, King Arthur closed his helmet so that the two young knights would not know who he was.

When he had come close to the two knights, Sir Gawaine rode forward a short way to meet him. “Sir Knight,” he said, “you must know that this is truly dangerous ground that you have ridden into. There is no side road from here across the swamp, and you may not go forward without riding a tilt with me.”

“Sir Knight,” said King Arthur, “I am very willing to ride a tilt with you. But I will fight you only on one condition, and it is this: the one who is thrown down must serve the other fully for seven whole days.”
“I accept your challenge, Sir Knight,” said Sir Gawaine. For he said to himself, “Surely a knight as strong and skilled as I am will easily bring down this unknown knight.”

So each knight at once took his place. Each lowered his spear and readied his shield, made himself fully ready in every way, and rested for a short moment. Then each suddenly shouted to his horse, dug his spurs into its flanks, and rushed to the clash. Each knight struck the other in the middle of his defenses, and look! The spear of Sir Gawaine burst into pieces. But the spear of King Arthur held firm, so that Sir Gawaine was lifted right out of his saddle and over the back end of his horse. He fell into the dust with terrible force. He could not rise from that fall right away, but lay dazed for a little while. When he did get up, he saw that the white knight who had thrown him was sitting on his horse close beside him.
Then King Arthur spoke and said, “Sir Knight, I have completely beaten you, and so you must now serve me, as you promised on your knightly word.”

Then Sir Ewaine, who sat on his horse nearby, spoke up. “Not so, Sir Knight,” he said. “Not until you have dealt with me. I demand that you joust with me at once. If I throw you down, I will require you to release my cousin from the service he has promised. But if you throw me down, then I will serve you just as he has promised to serve you.”
“Sir Knight,” said King Arthur, “I accept your challenge with all my heart!”

So each knight took his place and made himself ready for the clash. Then they shouted and charged together, rushing at each other like two rams on a hillside. The spear of Sir Ewaine was also shattered into pieces. But King Arthur’s spear held firm, so that the straps of Sir Ewaine’s saddle burst apart, and both the saddle and the knight were swept off the horse’s back with such force that a falling tower could not have made a greater noise than Sir Ewaine did when he hit the dust of that causeway.

Then Sir Ewaine got to his feet and stared at him, filled with amazement. King Arthur came to him and spoke to him like this: “Ha, Sir Knight, it seems to me that you have been fairly beaten today. And so, as you promised, both you and that other knight must carry out all my commands for the next seven whole days. This is the command that I give to you both: you must go at once to the Lady Guinevere at Cameliard and bring her the greeting of her knight. Tell her that her knight, to whom she gave her necklace, has sent you, who are sons of kings, to do her service. And everything that she commands you to do in these next seven days, you must do down to the smallest detail.”

“Sir Knight,” said Sir Gawaine, “we will do as you command, since we have pledged ourselves to it. But when these seven days are over, I swear that I will seek you out and fight this combat to the very end. Any knight may be knocked from his horse, as I have been, yet I believe I may do better against you if I fight you with all my strength.”
“Sir Knight,” said King Arthur, “it shall be just as you wish. Yet I truly believe that when these seven days are over, you will not want to fight me as much as you do now.”

After saying this, King Arthur saluted the two knights, and they saluted him. Then he turned his horse and went on his way. Whenever he thought of how those two good knights had fallen before his attack, and how astonished and ashamed they had been at their defeat, he laughed aloud with pure fun. He promised himself that he had never in all his life taken part in so joyful an adventure as this.
When Sir Ewaine had mended the straps of his saddle, he and Sir Gawaine mounted their horses and set out toward Cameliard, very low in spirits.
Then the miller came out of the mill once more. He was greatly delighted to have watched such a wonderful knightly fight from so safe a place as the one where he had stood.

So King Arthur rode onward, very contented in his mind, until the afternoon was growing late. By that time he had come close to the arm of the forest that he had chosen as the proper place to leave his horse and his armor.

As he drew near this edge of the forest, he saw before him at the roadside a gnarled and stunted oak tree. He saw that a shield hung upon the oak, and that beneath the shield these words were written in fair, large letters:

“Whoever strikes this shield
Does so at the risk of his life.”
Then King Arthur felt a great spirit rise in him. He raised his spear and struck that shield so hard that it rang like thunder.

At once King Arthur heard a voice come out of the forest, crying, “Who has dared to attack my shield?” And immediately a large knight rode out from the trees upon a white horse, just like the one King Arthur himself rode. The trappings of the horse and of the knight were all white, like those of King Arthur and his horse. The knight wore on his helmet, as his crest, a swan with outspread wings. On his shield he bore the emblem of three swans on a silver field. From the crest and the emblem on the shield, King Arthur knew that this knight was Sir Pellias, who had come with him from Camelot to Tintagalon.

When Sir Pellias had come close to where King Arthur waited for him, he pulled up his horse and spoke to him in a very stern voice. “Ho! Ho! Sir Knight,” he said. “Why did you dare to strike my shield? Truly, that blow will bring you great danger and sorrow. Now get ready to defend yourself at once, because of what you have done.”

“Wait! Wait! Sir Knight,” said King Arthur. “It shall be as you wish, and I will fight you. But I will not try this adventure until you agree that the knight who is beaten in the fight shall serve the other in whatever way the other may wish, for one week from this time.”
“Sir Knight,” said Sir Pellias, “I accept that risk. So I now tell you to get ready for the fight at once.”

Then each knight took his place and set his spear and shield. When they were ready, they charged at each other at once, with a force like two stones hurled from a catapult. They met in the middle of the course, and once again King Arthur was entirely successful in his attack. The spear of Sir Pellias burst into pieces, but the spear of King Arthur held firm. Sir Pellias was thrown from his saddle with terrible force, more than half a spear’s length behind the rear of his horse. He did not fully recover from that fall for a long time. King Arthur had to wait beside him for quite a while before he was able to lift himself from the ground where he lay.

“Ha! Sir Knight,” said King Arthur, “it has surely gone badly for you today. You have been completely overthrown, and now you must keep your pledge to serve me for seven days. So I command you to go at once to Cameliard and greet the Lady Guinevere from me. Tell her that her knight, the one to whom she gave her necklace, has won the fight against you. I also command you to obey her for seven days in whatever she may order you to do.”

“Sir Knight,” said Sir Pellias, “it shall be just as you order. But I wish I knew who you are, for I declare that in all my life I have never been overthrown as you have overthrown me. Indeed, I think there are very few men in the world who could have done to me what you have done.”
“Sir Knight,” said King Arthur, “some day you shall know who I am. But for now I am bound to complete secrecy.”
Then he saluted Sir Pellias, turned, rode into the forest, and was gone.
Sir Pellias mounted his horse and went to Cameliard, very downcast and troubled in spirit. He wondered greatly who that knight could be, who had treated him as he had just been treated.

That day four knights came to Cameliard: first Sir Geraint, then Sir Gawaine and Sir Ewaine, and last of all Sir Pellias. When these four saw one another, they were all so ashamed that hardly one of them dared to look another in the face. They came before the Lady Guinevere and explained their situation to her. They told her how the knight who wore her necklace had overthrown them all and sent them there to serve her for a week. She considered how great and famous those four knights were in deeds of chivalry, and she was overjoyed that her knight had proved himself so great in the feats of arms he had set out to perform. But she wondered greatly who that champion could be, and she turned the question over in her own mind. For it was entirely unheard of that one knight, in one day, with a single spear, should have overthrown five such proven and famous knights as Duke Mordaunt of North Umber, Sir Geraint, Sir Gawaine, Sir Ewaine, and Sir Pellias. So she was very glad that she had given her necklace to such a worthy knight. She felt extraordinary pleasure and pride at the thought of the honor he had brought her.

After King Arthur had entered the forest, he soon came to the place where the woodcutters mentioned earlier were at their work. He stayed with them that night. When the next morning came, he left his horse and armor in their care, telling them to guard these things carefully and that they would be wonderfully rewarded for it. Then he left that place, meaning to return to Cameliard. He wore the rough jerkin of coarse cloth that he had worn ever since he left Tintagalon.

When he reached the edge of the forest, he put his cap of disguise on his head and so took on his humble appearance once more. With his knightly rank hidden completely, he returned to Cameliard to be the gardener’s boy, as he had been before.
